body: Thursday, March 13 2025 — Macro · Sectors · Flows · Crypto
Information available before 2025-03-13 00:00 UTC. Prices use completed prior sessions. Prepared retrospectively; later outcomes are excluded.

Macro Stance: The S&P 500 closed at 5,599.30 on the prior close, 7.73% lower over 20 sessions, and the Nasdaq 100 is down 9.67% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Bloomberg counted $1.1 trillion of Nasdaq 100 value shed as the tech meltdown spread [1], and CNBC put more than $750 billion of megacap tech value lost in the worst Nasdaq day since 2022 [2]. Recession odds have moved into the mainstream: J.P. Morgan's economist puts the chance at 40% [3], and Citi has downgraded US stocks [4]. Goldman Sachs cut its year-end S&P 500 target to 6,200 on weaker profit forecasts [5], and MarketWatch framed the start of the term as the worst since 2009 [6]. The damage is tariff-led rather than credit-led, which is why equities are falling while Treasuries rally.

Rates & Curve: The 2Y closed at 4.01% and the 10Y at 4.32% on the prior close (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12). The 10Y-2Y spread is +31 bps and the 10Y-3M spread is -3 bps. Over 20 observations the 2Y fell 28 bps and the 10Y fell 22 bps, which lifts the 10Y-2Y spread by 6 bps. The curve is positively sloped, and the 20-observation move is bull steepening, with both yields down and the 2Y down more. Over five observations both yields rose, the 2Y 2 bps and the 10Y 4 bps, so the rally is a month-long move rather than a one-week trade (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12). Equity context is the mirror image: the VIX closed at 24.23, up 51.25% over 20 sessions from a 16.02 reference (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), while the dollar index at 103.61 is 4.03% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

New / Most Important: The latest hard print is February inflation at 2.8%, lower than expected [7], and the New York Times framed it as easing more than forecast [8]. Payrolls rose 151,000 in February, less than expected [9], and Bloomberg read the jobs data as evidence the labour market is softening [10]. Powell said the Fed is in no hurry to adjust rates [11], and the Fed's Waller sees cuts this year but not this month [12]. The fiscal side is the live risk: the House passed a stopgap, and Senate Democrats are fuming as the shutdown deadline nears [13]. On trade, Trump said he would double Canadian steel and aluminium tariffs from 25% to 50% [14] and then halted the step after Ontario suspended its electricity price hikes [15]. Mexico will not pay tariffs on USMCA goods until April 2, Trump said [16], and the auto industry is pleading for certainty as April 2 tariffs loom [17].

Playbook ✓: Stay underweight high-beta US growth until the stopgap clears the Senate and the tariff calendar stops moving. Keep duration as the hedge while the curve bull-steepens, and add to equities only when the VIX falls back toward its 16.02 reference from 20 sessions earlier. Be ready to cover if the S&P 500 reclaims 6,068.50, its level 20 sessions ago (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). What would change the call is a clean stopgap plus a Fed that keeps the cut debate open without moving the pause earlier.

Macro Stance: Germany's spending package is the pivot for the euro area. Euronews framed the early-March reaction as a 'whatever it takes' moment that sparked a market rally [18], and Politico gave Merz two weeks to deliver a historic spending revolution [19]. EU ministers have backed a temporary exemption for defense spending from EU budget rules [20]. The STOXX Europe 600 closed at 541.25, down 1.19% over 20 sessions, but the DAX is up 2.39% over the same span and gained 1.56% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The euro is 5.30% stronger over 20 sessions against the dollar, at 1.0914 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Credit & Inflation: The inflation side is the caution. Lagarde warned that trade and defense shocks could amplify euro-zone inflation [21], and that higher defense spending could push inflation up [22]. The Bundesbank called the German spending justified but not a cure-all [23]. Bond markets are pricing the supply: Reuters said the German spending boost will leave a lasting imprint on world bond markets [24], and Bloomberg tied Italy's bond worries to Meloni's strategy from defense to banks [25]. Euro-area unemployment at 6.2% [26] leaves room for the fiscal push to show up in growth before it shows up in prices.

New / Most Important: The newest signal is the exemption itself: EU ministers back a temporary carve-out from the bloc's deficit rules for defense [20], while Germany rejected defense Eurobonds in favour of funding joint projects through the EU budget [27]. The Wall Street Journal's piece on overlooked European defense stocks as a hedge-fund home run shows where the positioning has gone [28].

Playbook ✓: Overweight defense and infrastructure supply chains over autos, which remain a tariff trade. Keep the add sized small until the Bund curve shows whether the spending is inflationary, and cut the European cyclical exposure if long yields rise faster than the spending pipeline. The call breaks if the DAX gives back its 20-session gain while the STOXX 600 holds its lower base.

Macro Stance: Beijing set the 2025 growth target at around 5% [29], but economists say it needs much stronger stimulus if the US trade war intensifies [30], and officials have said more support is possible if growth slows [31]. The price data is the weak spot: China's inflation slipped below zero for the first time in a year [32], and consumer prices fell in February [33]. Bloomberg's read is that China is struggling to escape a deflation cycle [34], and CNN's line is that the deflation problem is getting worse [35]. The policy response so far is modest, so each stimulus headline trades as a one-day event rather than a regime change.

PMIs & Activity: The official non-manufacturing PMI printed 50.4 in February [36], and Reuters reported that factory activity picked up while trade uncertainty weighed [37]. The external leg is weaker. CNBC reported exports missed forecasts as US tariffs hit, with imports posting their sharpest fall since July 2023 [38], and SCMP described imports and exports cooling as tariffs cast a chill over trade [39]. Car sales rose 1.3% in the first two months of 2025 [40], which is the consumer side of the activity read: positive, but not a boom. Read growth from the PMIs and the credit data together, not from the export headline alone.

Credit Impulse: The newest credit signal is tightening at the margin rather than a loan surge. Some Hong Kong banks are refusing home loans for Vanke's Le Mont project [41], and China's bond yields jumped to three-month highs as investors pared rate-cut expectations [42]. A strategist warned that more Chinese bond issuance, used to keep yields up, will drain liquidity from markets [43]. A genuine credit impulse would show as a new-loans print that beats its year-earlier pace, plus a PBOC rate cut rather than liquidity injections alone. Until then the credit leg argues for tactical rather than structural exposure.

Property: Property is still shrinking, and the policy support is incremental. SCMP's analysts say the push for better-quality homes adds stress for developers [44]. China Evergrande and others were ordered to repay $1.8 bln of deposit pledges to a property unit [45]. The property minister says the sector is showing positive changes [46], and Reuters relays Bloomberg's report that Beijing is weighing an end to the price cap on local-government apartment purchases [47]. Those are the right directions, but none of them reverses the inventory problem on its own.

Fiscal, Policy & Trade: Fiscal support is at the margin: a $41 billion consumption plan is described as only a start while deflationary pressure deepens [48]. The trade front is active on both sides. China's extra tariffs of up to 15% on major US farm exports [49] have taken effect for agricultural products [50], and the WSJ reported Walmart drew an earful from China over its response to Trump's tariffs [51]. The one big policy catalyst is diplomatic: Washington and Beijing are discussing a Trump-Xi summit for June [52].

Markets & Flows: Hong Kong has led the policy rally. The Hang Seng closed at 23,600.31, up 7.97% over 20 sessions though down 0.76% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). KWEB is up 8.93% and FXI up 9.03% over the same span, while the CSI 300 tracker ASHR gained 2.27% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The Shanghai Composite is up just 0.76% at 3,371.92 index points (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Flows are split: Reuters reported hedge funds cut China stocks for a fourth week as DeepSeek optimism faded [53], while CNBC reported mainland investors bought a record amount of Hong Kong stocks to play AI [54]. The yuan is the quiet tell: USD/CNY at 7.2591 is 0.66% lower over 20 sessions, and the offshore yuan climbed to a four-month high [55]. The US listings show the same fear: Alibaba's ADR discount, which Yahoo Finance tied to fear of US-China decoupling [56], is the cleanest gauge of how much of the policy rally is priced offshore.

New / Most Important: The new item is Beijing's pressure on a US retailer and the rotation it signals. Chinese authorities summoned Walmart over reported supplier price-cut demands [57], and Citi downgraded US stocks while raising China as the America First trade fades [58]. The AP's read of the annual Congress was that China ended it with questions open over how to revive its slowing economy [59], so the policy response is still being designed.

Playbook ✓: Own China policy beta through Hong Kong internet and the broad ETF proxies into the June summit window, and keep the size small because the domestic cycle is not turning. Avoid developers and bank credit until the loan data turns, and treat a Hang Seng close under its 20-session reference of 21,857.92 as the sign the policy rally has failed (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). ⚠ Divergence: Hong Kong equities rose 7.97% over 20 sessions while consumer prices fell and exports slowed, so the rally is running ahead of the data.

Macro Stance: Japan's growth picture is weaker than first reported. Reuters says fourth-quarter GDP was revised lower as US tariffs cloud the outlook [60], and the WSJ notes the economy grew more slowly than first estimated [61]. Against that, the policy debate is tilting toward a hike. Sources say inflation risks may bring a BOJ rate-hike discussion in May [62], and the economy minister says Japan is ready to declare an end to deflation [63]. Wage bargaining is the evidence: the largest union group is seeking the biggest wage hike demand in more than 30 years [64], and major firms have agreed to big pay increases [65]. Japan's trade minister still has no assurance of a tariff exemption from Washington [66].

Activity & Currency: USD/JPY closed at 148.0420, up 0.66% in the prior session but down 3.08% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), after the yen hit a five-month high on expectations of a BOJ hike [67]. The Nikkei 225 closed at 36,819.09, flat in the prior session and down 5.11% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The bond market is the story. The 10-year yield hit its highest since 2008 on bets for BOJ hikes [68], and Japanese 10-year yields surged to near 16-year highs in early March [69]. Investors boosted domestic bond holdings and sold foreign stocks in February [70], and Reuters reported services sentiment has soured on the cost of living [71]. Corporate capex fell for the first time in four years amid tariff fears [72].

Playbook ✓: Hold yen-hedged Japanese exposure over outright long Nikkei risk while the JGB curve is repricing. Add yen on a clear BOJ signal toward a May hike, and treat a Nikkei close under its 20-session reference of 38,801.17 as the sign that domestic equities are not yet pricing the rate path (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Banks are the transmission: the BOJ is scrutinising how rising rates hit deposits [73], which keeps the financials leg sensitive to any policy surprise.

Macro Stance: The RBA has already cut. The AFR published the chart the central bank used to justify its latest cut [74], and ABC asked what the cut means for savers [75]. Growth looks firmer on paper: fourth-quarter GDP rose 1.3%, CNBC reported [76], and TradingView called it a two-year high [77]. The external risk is live. Anthony Albanese called US tariffs 'not a friendly act' after Donald Trump refused an exemption for Australia [78], and ABC framed how a US recession could hit Australia [79]. The ASX 200 closed at 7,786.20, down 1.32% in the prior session and 8.78% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Demand & Financing: AUD/USD closed at 0.6295, up 0.25% in the prior session and down 0.05% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Household wealth looks strong on paper: national housing values surged to a record $11.032 trillion even as Sydney and Melbourne lost value [80]. Costs are rising at the household level, with power prices set to rise nearly 9 per cent for some from mid-year [81]. Financing is where the pressure shows. BlackRock cut its exposure to Australian shares, citing poor value [82], and Commonwealth Bank is down 12.76% over 20 sessions at 144.80 AUD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so the bank leg is the weak point of the index.

Playbook ✓: Stay underweight Australian banks and broad domestic beta until the ASX 200 reclaims its 20-session reference of 8,535.30 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Keep AUD exposure hedged against a US-recession leg, since the currency is a tariff proxy rather than a rate story, and revisit once the RBA's cuts show up in bank margins rather than in housing values alone.

Macro Stance: Poland is a strong-zloty, cooling-housing story. Bloomberg tied the zloty's surge to a 10-year high against the dollar to a hawkish central bank [83], and Bankier asked who is hurt by a currency that is strong as it has been only once in history [84]. Inflation is the drag on rate relief: Business Insider Polska wrote that inflation will still rise, a strong argument for the RPP on rates [85], and GUS said January CPI edged up [86]. Growth firmed: the fourth-quarter GDP reading showed acceleration but fell short of expectations [87]. The labour market is the bright spot, with Eurostat putting Poland at the lowest unemployment rate on record [88], and GUS reporting wages for 2024 [89].

Markets: USD/PLN closed at 3.8407, down 0.76% in the prior session and 4.56% over 20 sessions, while EUR/PLN is at 4.1917 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Strefa Inwestorów noted the euro is at its cheapest since 2018 as the zloty gains [90]. Equities lag the currency: the WIG20 total-return tracker closed at 49.89 PLN, up 2.21% over 20 sessions, and the dollar-based MSCI Poland ETF EPOL is up 7.99% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Leadership is rotating. Bankier reported speculators moving from the Ukrainian names into steel and defense stocks [91], and Dino Polska's shares reached a record high [92]. PKO is up 2.02% over 20 sessions at 71.64 PLN, while Bank Pekao is down 0.63% at 173.80 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The currency's gains come in bursts: Rzeczpospolita reported a zloty sell-off on Monday as the dollar and euro rose sharply [93].

Fiscal & Politics: Brussels is easing its excessive-deficit rules, and Rzeczpospolita asked whether Poland wins or loses [94]; Credit Agricole's chief economist for Poland said the EU is moving toward looser fiscal rules [95]. Domestic politics are the live risk. Premier Tusk said the government's confidence vote will take place on 11 June [96], and Bloomberg reported a far-right candidate jumping to second in the presidential race [97]. Talks on changing an important tax are under way, and officials say a compromise is needed [98]. The US warned it would retaliate if Poland introduces a tax on big tech [99]. A report on Ukrainian migrants puts their net contribution to the budget at PLN 15.21 billion [100], which reframes the fiscal argument.

Corporate & Sectors: Orlen set a record for gas output that covers half of Poland's demand [101], and Reuters reported Naftogaz and Orlen will cooperate on LNG [102]. The stock is up 15.99% over 20 sessions at 66.17 PLN (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Banks are the policy target: Business Insider Polska wrote that big profits have become inconvenient and banks are once again the punching bag [103], and falling deposit rates are letting banks earn billions [104]. KGHM's new management says years of neglect and under-investment left the miner behind [105], and the stock is down 4.19% over 20 sessions at 129.15 PLN. Index plumbing matters too: CCC and Żabka enter the WIG20 after the 21 March session, while Cyfrowy Polsat and JSW leave [106].

Geopolitics & Security: Warsaw is building its defense posture in public. Poland asked NATO to raise the defence spending minimum to 3% of GDP [107], and the premier said Poland must look at nuclear options after Trump's stance [108]. The military plan includes 100,000 volunteers in training by 2027 [109], and the reserve pool is above 300 thousand people [110]. Security incidents are concrete: prosecutors say Russia posed a spy as a Belarusian refugee to set a Warsaw mall on fire [111]. The defense push is also a budget question, with the Polish president asking NATO leaders to increase military spending [112].

New / Most Important: The signal that matters is the fiscal and defense pivot taken together. Brussels' easing of deficit rules [94] lets Warsaw fund defense without a sharp consolidation, while the RPP debate has shifted toward relief for borrowers [113]. Parkiet's line that this is 'not a time for emotion' from the RPP [114] signals the central bank will not rush. Falling mortgage instalments [115] help households but cut the interest income banks rely on, which is why the tax talks matter for the lenders.

Playbook ✓: Own the zloty against the euro on dips while the RPP stays on hold, and keep bank exposure sized to the tax debate rather than the rate cycle. Treat defense names as a fiscal-floor trade rather than a growth story, and trim into strength. ⚠ Divergence: the WIG20 total-return tracker is up only 2.21% over 20 sessions while Warsaw and Kraków apartment prices fell year on year for the first time in three years [116], so the equity leg is lagging the housing signal.

Narrative: The AI build-out still anchors technology earnings, but the tape has turned on valuation and recession risk. XLK is down 10.43% over 20 sessions at 211.68 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), after the Nasdaq 100 shed $1.1 trillion as the tech meltdown spread [1]. Nvidia lost $1 trillion of market value and is down 20% for the year [117]. The flow that matters now is positioning: investors bought a Magnificent 7 ETF during the downturn, per Reuters [118], so the megacap dip is being bought rather than sold.

Reported: Oracle's sales missed estimates even as its chief executive pointed to AI-driven growth [119], and Marvell fell nearly 20% after an outlook that fell short of high expectations [120]. Intel named Lip-Bu Tan chief executive [121], and the shares rose 4.55% in the prior session (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

EPS Upside Watch: Memory is the set-up for an upside surprise. Seeking Alpha's case is a prolonged memory cycle for Micron [122], and Micron rose 7.40% in the prior session at 95.64 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so pricing is moving in its favor.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Dip-buying cuts against the consensus that AI is losing momentum: investors bought the Magnificent 7 ETF amid the downturn [118]. That is a flow signal rather than an earnings one, and it can reverse quickly if guidance cuts like Oracle's and Marvell's spread to the rest of the group.

Narrative: Communication services has lost its defensive edge. XLC is down 6.33% over 20 sessions at 96.83 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Meta is down 13.93% over the same span at 619.56 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Yahoo Finance headlined Meta's fall on the day [123], and Alphabet is down 9.83% over 20 sessions even as it pitches small-reactor nuclear as a cost fix [124].

Reported: Telecom had the sector's sharpest near-term drop. Telecom stocks fell after Verizon's comments at a Deutsche Bank conference [125], and AT&T and T-Mobile tumbled on the same day [126]. Verizon is still up 5.19% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so the damage is to the near-term outlook rather than the trend.

EPS Upside Watch: Little earnings upside is set up. The Alphabet case is a cost story: its CIO says the company aims to slash the cost of new nuclear through small reactor deployments [124], which helps the power bill more than the top line. Stocktwits framed the Verizon and AT&T slide as a split retail view [127], which keeps the crowd divided rather than long.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Disney's stock sank under sagging consumer sentiment [128], which cuts against the defensive-entertainment view that households keep paying for streaming when budgets tighten. The sector is a consumer story, not a growth one, and the price action says so.

Narrative: Banks are priced for a recession scare. XLF is down 7.49% over 20 sessions at 47.68 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Citigroup, Goldman Sachs and SoFi were hit hard in the Monday selloff [129]. Citi's downgrade of US stocks [4] and the rising recession fears behind the bank selloff [130] set the narrative.

Reported: No major bank reported in the window. The fresh sell-side datapoint is Goldman's year-end S&P 500 target cut to 6,200 [5], which signals marked-down profit forecasts. Hedge funds are also de-risking, Reuters reported [131], which is a headwind for trading desks.

EPS Upside Watch: The upside case is narrow. Mortgage rates fell to their lowest level this year [132], which helps lending volumes, and hedge funds have Capital One on their undervalued list [133]. That is a stock-picker call rather than an earnings preview.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Credit is calmer than equities: HYG is down only 0.65% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so the bank selloff is about recession and rates rather than a credit event, which cuts against the banks-in-trouble framing.

Narrative: Oil trades on supply and China demand, not on the equity tape. WTI closed at 67.68 USD, up 2.16% in the prior session but down 7.69% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Vitol's chief executive warned that China demand concerns and GDP growth threaten oil prices [134], and Gunvor's said global supply growth is outstripping demand [135]. XLE is down 3.79% over 20 sessions at 87.78 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).
Reported: Energy has no fresh earnings in the window, so the reported datapoint is the weekly inventory print: crude stockpiles rose while gasoline and distillates saw big draws [136].

EPS Upside Watch: Gas is the upside leg. Henry Hub closed at 4.08 USD, up 16.06% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and OilPrice reported natural gas prices at two-year highs as geopolitical tensions rose [137]. That helps the producers more than the majors.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Canada could restrict its oil exports to the US if the trade war escalates [138]. That is a supply threat from a trading partner, which cuts against the oversupply story that the Vitol and Gunvor comments set up [135].

Narrative: Industrials are split between data-centre power and tariff-exposed manufacturing. XLI is down 6.13% over 20 sessions at 130.11 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Eaton is buying Fibrebond for $1.4 billion to deepen its data-centre business [139], which is the part of the sector still growing.

Reported: Boeing's February deliveries rose 63% from a year earlier [140], while rising costs and supply-chain risks from tariffs are the counterweight [141]. Boeing is down 11.99% over 20 sessions at 158.80 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

EPS Upside Watch: The set-up is volume. Boeing's February deliveries, up sharply from a year earlier [140], give it a volume tailwind into its next report, and Hitachi Energy's $250M commitment against a transformer shortage [142] shows the grid capex that feeds the electrical-equipment makers.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Tariffs push airframe costs up. AerCap's chief said a 787 could rise by $40 million in the worst case [143], which cuts against the volume story and shows why deliveries alone do not settle the earnings case.

Narrative: Consumer discretionary is the weakest cyclical. XLY is down 11.73% over 20 sessions at 197.53 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Forbes reported that four major US airlines cut forecasts citing a dip in consumer confidence [144]. Tariffs and sentiment are the drivers, and the price action is the confirmation.

Reported: Target issued a rough first-quarter profit warning on tariffs [145], and its shares are down 19.00% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Kohl's shares plunged 20% on a rough outlook [146], and American Eagle said the consumer is slowing and issued weak guidance [147].

EPS Upside Watch: The upside is thin. Home Depot is down 12.40% over 20 sessions at 364.73 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Stifel's downgrade ahead of the report reset expectations [148]. The only bull case is that low expectations make a guidance hold a positive surprise.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Retail holders are not walking away from Tesla: Business Insider reported that with the stock cut in half, investors want their CEO back [149]. Tesla is down 24.48% over 20 sessions at 248.09 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so a consumer-weak sector is being held by the crowd at the same time as the consensus avoids it.

Narrative: Staples are not as defensive as they look. XLP fell 2.17% in the prior session and is down 1.13% over 20 sessions at 79.70 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Costco had its biggest one-day drop in more than three years [150] after its quarterly profit missed market expectations [151].

Reported: Costco is down 12.40% over 20 sessions at 927.08 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). PepsiCo and Conagra asked to exempt some imports from tariffs [152], and the North American coffee industry is seeking answers amid the trade war [153].

EPS Upside Watch: Pricing is the upside lever. The DOJ is investigating major egg producers amid soaring prices [154], and Axios says consumers remain willing to pay [155]. Pricing power in staples depends on that same willingness to pay.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Walmart is not defensive where its supply chain is contested: Chinese authorities summoned the retailer over reported supplier price-cut demands [57]. That cuts against the view that big-box staples are insulated from trade policy.

Narrative: Healthcare is a sector of two stories. XLV is down 0.98% over 20 sessions at 144.60 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and the obesity-drug trade decides the tone. Novo Nordisk fell 6.3% after its next-generation trial disappointed [156], and Roche's $5.3 billion obesity deal with Zealand Pharma pushed Novo lower again [157].

Reported: Eli Lilly plans to launch its weight-loss drug in emerging markets this year [158]. Novo's Danish shares are down 13.33% over 20 sessions at 507.60 DKK (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

EPS Upside Watch: Pricing is the test for revenue. Novo's chief executive warned that tariffs could send the prices of Ozempic and Wegovy higher [159], which would support revenue even if volume slows.

⚡ Breaking Convention: The cheap-GLP-1 story is losing support. A judge ruled against a compounding group and Hims & Hers' shares fell [160], and Hims shut its dermatology business [161], so the compounding channel is under legal pressure while the branded makers hold the narrative.

Narrative: Materials split on the metal. XLB is down 4.85% over 20 sessions at 84.93 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Copper futures are up 4.93% over 20 sessions at 4.82 USD a pound (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and the US is weighing a 25 percent tariff on copper imports [162]. Gold is up only 0.48% over 20 sessions at 2,946.80 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).
Reported: BHP is ready to invest $25M in copper explorer Cobre [163], a sign that miners are still financing copper supply.

EPS Upside Watch: Copper supply is tight at the margin. Chinese users are turning to off-exchange Congolese copper to ease supply tightness [164], which supports the price for miners with a cost advantage.
⚡ Breaking Convention: Gold ticked lower on the US inflation print [165], which cuts against the safe-haven story that gold should rally whenever recession fears spike.

Narrative: Real estate is rate-sensitive, and rates have just rallied. XLRE is down 1.87% over 20 sessions at 41.47 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Mortgage rates have fallen to their lowest point this year [132], and Bloomberg says US homebuyers face a new wild card this year: Trump [166].

Reported: Data-centre real estate is the reporting story. The question in the window was whether the data-centre REIT honeymoon period is over [167], which is a valuation question rather than an earnings one.

EPS Upside Watch: Lower mortgage rates support turnover, and that is the set-up for transaction-linked real-estate earnings. The bond rally is doing the work: the 10-year is 22 bps lower over 20 observations (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12).

⚡ Breaking Convention: Data-centre REITs are being questioned even as power demand grows [167]. The rate rally is not lifting the whole sector, which argues for picking housing-linked names rather than the index.

Narrative: Utilities are the power-demand hedge. XLU is down 2.80% over 20 sessions at 77.17 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), but the story is grid demand and the trade war's electricity front. NPR reported the US buys electricity from Canada, which is now a focus of the trade war [168].

Reported: Ontario slapped a 25% tax increase on electricity exports to the US in response to the trade war [169], Ontario then suspended its electricity price hikes, and Trump halted the doubling of metals tariffs in response [15]. Utilities are a political target as well as a grid story.

EPS Upside Watch: Grid capex is the earnings driver. Hitachi Energy committed $250M to address the transformer shortage [142], and Utility Dive wrote that growing electricity demand needs new policy solutions [170].

⚡ Breaking Convention: Utilities may subsidize data-centre growth by shifting costs to other ratepayers, a Harvard Law paper argues [171]. That is a political risk to the regulated return, which cuts against the view of utilities as a bond proxy.

Narrative: European autos are a tariff trade. The iShares European autos ETF is flat over 20 sessions at 52.38 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and automakers are bracing for higher costs as steel and aluminium tariffs kick in [172]. BMW is up 10.55% over 20 sessions at 84.28 EUR, but it will absorb tariff costs on some Mexican-built models [173].

Reported: Volkswagen expects 2025 revenue to rise as tariffs loom [174], but its profit is under pressure from tariffs and competition [175]. Porsche's earnings per share were cut by a third in 2024 [176].

EPS Upside Watch: Volkswagen's preferred shares are the upside set-up: up 17.29% over 20 sessions at 109.95 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and the company says revenue grows in 2025 [174]. The set-up is revenue recovery, not margin recovery.

⚡ Breaking Convention: Volkswagen and Stellantis evaded Trump's 25% tariffs [177], which cuts against the sector bear case. The bear case still holds on margins, which is why the stance stays bearish while the revenue read is mixed.

Narrative: Semis are split between AI demand and Asian supply competition. SOXX is down 10.83% over 20 sessions at 196.08 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), but gained 2.06% in the prior session. Intel named Lip-Bu Tan chief executive [121], and Reuters reported TSMC pitched Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom on a foundry joint venture for Intel [178].

Reported: Marvell's shares tumbled despite strong AI revenue growth [179], and the stock is down 35.99% over 20 sessions at 69.85 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Nvidia's 30% sell-off has left the shares cheaper than when ChatGPT launched, by one metric [180].
EPS Upside Watch: Memory is the sharpest upside. Micron is positioned for a prolonged memory cycle [122], and the stock is up 1.66% over 20 sessions at 95.64 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

⚡ Breaking Convention: China is building around US chips. Huawei reportedly acquired two million Ascend 910 AI chips from TSMC through shell companies [181], and a Chinese team won an award for replacing an Nvidia GPU with an industrial chip [182]. That cuts against the view that US chip leadership is unchallenged.

Rewarded: Rheinmetall expects robust 2025 sales [183] and sees a profit jump as Europe prepares for a military spending surge [184]. The stock rose 9.62% in the prior session at 1,265.00 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Volkswagen's guidance that revenue will rise in 2025 [174] has its preferred shares up 17.29% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Air France-KLM's shares jumped on an earnings beat and growth expectations [185]. Both moves came with growth attached rather than cost cuts, which is the pattern the next block is built on.

Punished: Target shares are down 19.00% over 20 sessions after a first-quarter profit warning on tariffs [145]. Kohl's shares plunged 20% on a rough outlook [146], and Delta cut its outlook, with the stock falling after the company cited 'macro uncertainty' [186]. Costco fell 11.52% over five sessions after its quarterly profit missed expectations [151], and Marvell dropped nearly 20% when its outlook fell short of high expectations [120], a 22.51% fall over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Pattern: The sorting variable is guidance, not the quarter. Oracle's sales missed estimates even as its chief executive pointed to AI-driven growth [119], and Marvell's strong AI revenue growth did not prevent a 35.99% fall over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Consumer names that cut outlooks on tariffs fell hardest, while the one name that guided up on defense demand was rewarded.

Attention into EPS: The next reaction set-up is Nio's fourth-quarter report on March 21 [187], which will test the China EV read-across after Tesla's trouble in China [188]. For the US consumer, the Costco and Target reactions set the bar for the next consumer print.

Playbook: Sell the guide, not the beat. Do not buy a stock on a quarter beat when the guidance is cut, and wait for the guidance-driven drawdown to stabilise before adding. Guidance raisers in defense are the funding leg for the sector rotation. The call is invalidated by a second guidance cut in the same sector inside a month.

Attention Gap: The Trump administration is seeking minerals refining on Pentagon bases, Reuters reported [189], and Business Insider Polska asked whether Poland can join the rare-earth rush [190]. The US and Uzbekistan agreed a critical-minerals partnership [191], so the policy tailwind is real but the attention is scattered across small caps.

Exposure & Risk: The listed exposure is small and policy-driven. MP Materials is down 1.42% over 20 sessions at 24.34 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Lynas is up 2.47% over the same span at 7.06 AUD (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Liquidity and single-name concentration are the risks, and a headline about a Pentagon contract can move these names more than the metals do.

Trigger to Watch: A Pentagon siting or procurement decision would make this theme consensus. The MP Materials level to watch is its 20-session reference of 24.69 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Attention Gap: The US is weighing a 25 percent tariff on copper imports [162], and Chinese users are turning to off-exchange Congolese copper [164]. Grid demand is the buyer that gets less attention: Hitachi Energy committed $250M against a transformer shortage [142], and Eaton is spending $1.4 billion on Fibrebond to grow its data-centre business [139].

Exposure & Risk: Copper futures closed at 4.82 USD a pound, up 4.93% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), while the copper-miner ETF COPX is down 2.25% over the same span at 39.58 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The miners lag the metal, so the exposure is to the price rather than to equity leverage. Copper here is a grid and capex asset, not a read on China's growth.
Trigger to Watch: The tariff decision would make this theme consensus. Copper's 20-session reference is 4.59 USD a pound (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Attention Gap: Blackstone won SEC approval for a private credit interval fund [192], while Bloomberg reported that a private-credit pioneer was dragged down by insults and indecision [193]. An Australian lender kept gating redemptions while promoting its funds [194], and CNBC flagged a controversial private credit ETF facing new regulatory hurdles [195].

Exposure & Risk: Goldman says US credit spreads will get a lot wider amid tariffs [196], and Bloomberg wrote that a massive unwind makes US junk bonds a riskier bet than Europe's [197]. HYG is down 0.65% over 20 sessions at 78.96 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), while the investment-grade ETF LQD is up 0.32% at 107.66 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Trigger to Watch: HYG's 20-session reference is 79.48 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). A close below it would show the stress reaching liquid bonds, which is the point where the private-credit wrapper story becomes consensus.

Attention Gap: The 10-year JGB yield hit its highest level since 2008 on bets for BOJ hikes [68], and the BOJ is scrutinising how rising rates hit banks and deposits [73]. Brokers are rethinking repackaged JGBs after a regulator's warning [198].

Exposure & Risk: The listed exposure is EWJ, the Japan ETF, at 69.52 USD and up 1.13% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Yen strength is the transmission: USD/JPY at 148.0420 is 3.08% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so a hike would strengthen the currency while weighing on exporters' translated earnings.

Trigger to Watch: A BOJ rate-hike discussion in May would make this theme consensus [62]. The Nikkei 225 reference is 38,801.17 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and a close below it would show domestic equities failing to price the rate path.

Market Context: Bitcoin closed at 83,722.36 USD on the prior completed daily close, up 1.04% in the session but down 14.86% over 20 sessions from 98,333.94 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-12). Ether is down 30.34% over 20 sessions at 1,908.98, Solana 28.10%, Dogecoin 32.36% and XRP 16.73% (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-12). CNBC reported bitcoin falling to a November low under $80,000 on recession fears [199], and CoinDesk noted the CME gap fill as BTC dropped to $76,700 [200]. Chart watchers are focused on $74,000 [201] and on Fidelity's $70,000 support [202]. The spot ETF follows: IBIT is down 12.86% over 20 sessions at 47.15 USD (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-12).

New / Most Important: The reserve plan is the new policy hook, and it has not carried the crowd. Bitcoin fell as much as 6.5% after Trump's bitcoin reserve plan [203], and XRP holders are asking why the reserve excluded their coin [204]. Strategy plans to sell $21 billion of preferred stock [205], a new financing lever for the company whose shares trade as a bitcoin proxy, and MSTR is down 17.81% over 20 sessions at 262.55 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Coinbase fell 10% on crypto-summit disappointment and an S&P 500 snub [206], and the stock is down 28.16% over 20 sessions at 191.73 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Playbook: Avoid levered crypto equities (MSTR, COIN and the bitcoin miners) until bitcoin closes back above its 20-session reference of 98,333.94, the level that would signal the reserve trade is working (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-12). Ether is the more defensible leg only on a specific catalyst: Fidelity's request for staking approval on its ether ETF [207] is the one pending ether item. Dogecoin is the speculative tail, covered in the retail section, and it is not a Playbook holding.

Global Liquidity: Fed liquidity is on hold, with a cut bias for later. Powell said the Fed is in no hurry to adjust rates [11], and Reuters reported him signalling possible tweaks to the dot plot [208]. The Fed's Waller sees cuts this year but not this month [12]. The ECB published its strategy document, 'A robust strategy for a new era' [209], and the euro area's inflation worries now run through trade and defense shocks [21]. In China liquidity is tighter at the margin: a strategist says more Chinese bond issuance, used to keep yields up, will drain liquidity from markets [43]. The Nasdaq plans 24-hour trading five days a week [210], a structural change in when liquidity is available. Japan's yen is also the flow of the moment: a strategist calls it the new safe-haven currency [211].

Rates & Dollar: The 10-year closed at 4.32% (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12), 22 bps lower over 20 observations, and the 2-year at 4.01% fell 28 bps. The dollar index at 103.61 rose 0.16% in the prior session and is 4.03% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). CNBC reports the dollar is rising but remains pressured against peers with tariffs in focus [212], and The Guardian reports the euro and pound rose against the dollar amid 'Trumpcession' fears [213]. Duration is the clean hedge: TLT is up 1.62% over 20 sessions at 89.86 and IEF is up 1.67% at 94.43 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Credit Check: Credit is where the stress is showing. Bloomberg wrote that a massive unwind makes US junk bonds a riskier bet than Europe's [197], and Goldman says US credit spreads will get a lot wider amid tariffs [196]. HYG is down 0.65% over 20 sessions at 78.96 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), while LQD is up 0.32% at 107.66 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Private-credit wrappers are the new test: Blackstone won SEC approval for an interval fund [192], and an Australian lender was still gating redemptions [194].

Equity & Fund Flows: Dip-buying is the flow story. Reuters reported that investors bought a Magnificent 7 ETF amid the downturn [118]. Hedge funds sped up de-risking, and more is likely to come, Reuters says [131], while in Europe hedge funds fled positions and dented stock traders [214]. Millennium's $900 million loss is a sign of broader hedge-fund pain [215], and Goldman says hedge funds have given up half of their 2025 gains [216]. Options are the hedge: Moomoo reported put-option volume at a record high [217]. Retail is buying where institutions are selling: Investment Week reported that wealth managers ditched investment trusts as retail investors bought in droves [218], and Italy's asset managers saw net inflows double to 6 billion euros in February [219]. Buybacks are arriving at the small end, with Metropolitan Bank announcing a $50 million repurchase [220].

Portfolio Implication: Hold duration through TLT and IEF as the hedge, keep the dollar exposure tactical, and buy equity protection with puts while put volume is at a record. Avoid high-yield beta until HYG reclaims its 20-session reference of 79.48 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The portfolio change is to move from credit carry into Treasuries, and to add risk only after a clean stopgap vote and a steadier VIX. Currency hedges matter too: yen strength is the transmission channel to watch if the BOJ moves toward a May hike [62], and it would hit the Japanese equity leg.

What Is Priced: The market is pricing a political scare, not a fiscal break. The House passed a stopgap [221], and Senate Democrats are fuming as the shutdown deadline nears [13]. House leaders are holding their lines ahead of the vote [222]. The S&P 500 is down 7.73% over 20 sessions, while the VIX at 24.23 is up 51.25% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).

Conditional Expression: If the Senate passes the stopgap, the VIX should retrace toward its 16.02 reference and the equity drawdown should stop extending, with the trade shifting back to tariffs. If the Senate balks, the shutdown premium holds, the VIX stays elevated, and the Treasury rally carries on as the hedge.

Risk: The near-term damage falls on federal workers: Axios reported that the chaos will delay unemployment benefits for federal workers and the states [223]. The bigger risk is a stopgap that passes while the tariff calendar stays unresolved.

What Is Priced: Tariff timing is what the market is pricing. Mexico will not pay tariffs on USMCA goods until April 2, Trump said [16], and the auto industry is pleading for trade certainty as April 2 tariffs loom [17]. Canada will impose 25% reciprocal tariffs following US steel and aluminium duties [224], and Trump halted the plan to double Canadian metal tariffs to 50% [225].

Conditional Expression: If the tariff step set for April 2 proceeds [17], the auto and steel exposure in the European and Japanese names takes the cost hit first, which is why the autos stance stays bearish. If it is delayed again, the tariff premium fades in the Canadian and Mexican names and the VIX drifts back toward its reference.

Risk: The pattern is the risk. Trump has delayed and reversed tariffs in the window, with CNN reporting a one-month delay on tariffs for Mexico and Canada [226], so each reversal re-prices volatility rather than resolving it.

What Is Priced: A cut is priced for later in the year, not this month. The Fed's Waller sees cuts this year but not this month [12], and Powell said the Fed is in no hurry to adjust rates [11]. The curve has already moved: the 2-year is down 28 bps over 20 observations and the 10-year down 22 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12).

Conditional Expression: If the March pause is confirmed and the dot plot stays unchanged, the front end holds its gains and the bull steepening continues. If the Fed signals a higher-for-longer path, the 2-year gives back its 28 bps and the curve flattens, which is the bank-margin bear case.

Risk: Powell's comments left the forecast framework in play: Reuters reported him signalling possible tweaks to the dot plot of rate-path forecasts [208], so the next set of projections could move the market more than the decision itself.

What Is Priced: The market is pricing a German fiscal impulse with a defense carve-out. EU ministers back a temporary exemption for defense spending from the bloc's rules [20], and Merz has two weeks to deliver a historic spending revolution [19]. The DAX is up 2.39% over 20 sessions while the STOXX Europe 600 is down 1.19% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so Germany is running ahead of the region.

Conditional Expression: If the package passes on schedule, defense and infrastructure supply chains keep leading and the Bund curve steepens. If it stalls, the rally fades back toward the 20-session base, and the euro's 5.30% gain over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12) gives back ground.

Risk: Inflation and supply are the risks. Lagarde warned higher defense spending could push inflation up [22], and Reuters flagged that German spending surge worries loom over the Bund market [227]. The Bundesbank called the spending justified but not a cure-all [23].

Catalyst & Thesis: JPMorgan cut its Tesla price target and expects lower deliveries, Reuters reported [228], with Tesla's China shipments tumbling [229] and European sales down 45% [230]. Musk has launched an appeal to restore a $56 billion pay package [231]. The thesis is that the next delivery print is the catalyst, and the stock has already fallen far enough to make the miss visible.

Price Hurdle & Risk: The stock closed at 248.09 USD, up 7.59% in the prior session but down 24.48% over 20 sessions from 328.50 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Retail holders are not walking away [149], so a short into a strong bounce is the main risk.

Trade Expression: Bear call spread struck above the 20-session reference of 328.50, sized small. The trade is invalidated by a close above 328.50, which would mean the drawdown is over and the short is wrong.

Catalyst & Thesis: Nio's fourth-quarter report comes on March 21 [187]. The China EV backdrop is mixed: Fortune says Tesla is flailing in China and BYD's rapid rise is to blame [188], and China's car sales rose 1.3% in the first two months of the year [40]. The thesis is that a results beat on the EV volume line would validate the rally, while a miss would show the share gains are not sticking.

Price Hurdle & Risk: NIO closed at 5.10 USD, down 2.30% in the prior session but up 26.24% over 20 sessions from 4.04 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The five-session gain of 17.24% shows the rally is recent and momentum-led.
Trade Expression: Own NIO only into the results, sized small, with the 4.04 reference as the stop: a close below it erases the 20-session gain and invalidates the position.

Catalyst & Thesis: Intel named Lip-Bu Tan chief executive [121], and Reuters reported TSMC pitched an Intel foundry joint venture to Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom [178]. The thesis is that a foundry partner or joint venture would reset the turnaround, but the pitch is not yet a deal, so the stock has a catalyst that is still pending.

Price Hurdle & Risk: Intel closed at 20.68 USD, up 4.55% in the prior session and down 1.38% over 20 sessions from 20.97 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The five-session change of -0.62% shows the stock is not yet trending.

Trade Expression: Buy shares or calls only on a confirmed joint-venture announcement. Without it, the stock is a mixed hold around its 20-session reference of 20.97, and a close above that level confirms the rebound.

Catalyst & Thesis: The US and China are discussing a Trump-Xi summit for June [52], and Alibaba's AI reasoning model drove its shares higher [232]. Fear of decoupling shows in the ADR discount [56]. The thesis is that a summit lowers the decoupling premium and lets the AI model re-rate the stock.

Price Hurdle & Risk: BABA closed at 137.14 USD, down 1.35% in the prior session but up 21.60% over 20 sessions from 112.78 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The risk is a summit that slips, which would reopen the discount.
Trade Expression: Buy the ADR on pullbacks in two tranches. The trade is invalidated by a close back under 112.78, the 20-session base, which would mean the AI rally has failed.

Catalyst & Thesis: Orlen's record gas output, which covers half of Poland's demand [101], is the operating story, and its LNG cooperation with Naftogaz [102] gives it a supply role. The thesis is that a state-linked gas producer is less exposed to the trade war than the consumer names.

Price Hurdle & Risk: PKN closed at 66.17 PLN, up 4.58% over five sessions and 15.99% over 20 sessions from 57.05 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The political risk is the tax debate, which touches the energy names as well as the banks.
Trade Expression: Overweight Orlen against the WIG20 total-return tracker. The trade is invalidated by a close below 57.05, the 20-session reference.

Catalyst & Thesis: Strategy plans to sell $21 billion of preferred stock [205], and Coinbase's S&P 500 snub [206] shows how crowded the crypto-equity proxies are. The thesis is that a preferred sale to finance bitcoin exposure adds dilution risk while bitcoin is in a 20-session drawdown.

Price Hurdle & Risk: MSTR closed at 262.55 USD, up 0.75% in the prior session but down 14.91% over five sessions and 17.81% over 20 sessions from 319.46 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). A rebound toward the reference would be the main risk to the short.
Trade Expression: Short MSTR against long IBIT as a financing-risk spread. The trade is invalidated by a close above 319.46, the 20-session base.

Quantum computing is the trade pulling the most retail attention right now, and it rhymes with the 2023 Nvidia-led AI run, when the crowd moved from the bellwether into smaller names with the same story, the 2021 GameStop squeeze, and the 1999 infrastructure trade.

Why Retail Is Here: The story the crowd tells itself is simple: a machine that beats classical computing is close, and whoever owns the pure play gets the revolution without waiting for the megacaps to pick it up. D-Wave's breakthrough was the spark, and Yahoo Finance's headline is that the claim sent quantum stocks soaring [233], while Investopedia ran the same story for Wednesday's session [234]. Business Insider reported that quantum stocks rebounded from a dip after a new 'supremacy' announcement [235], so the dip is part of the appeal. The number the crowd anchors on is IonQ's 37.70 reference from February 11: at 21.82 the stock looks like a discount to where it traded a month earlier (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Yahoo Finance put the bigger question plainly: is quantum computing the next revolution after AI? [236]

What Is Driving It: The hard evidence starts with the prior session. IonQ rose 16.68% to 21.82 USD, Rigetti rose 11.18% to 8.95 and D-Wave rose 8.18% to 5.82 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Over five sessions IonQ is down 3.58% while Rigetti is up 9.41% and D-Wave up 3.93%. Over 20 sessions IonQ is down 42.12%, Rigetti down 18.78%, and D-Wave up 9.19%. The spread between them is the story: the pure play that lost the most is the one with the biggest one-day rebound. The backdrop is hostile to speculation: the Nasdaq 100 is down 9.67% over 20 sessions, the VIX closed at 24.23, and the 10-year sits at 4.32% after falling 22 bps over 20 observations (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12; US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12). Retail is buying a catalyst into a risk-off tape, which is why the moves are so large.

The Social Signal: Stocktwits reported that IonQ halted its at-the-market programme after a $372M raise, and that the stock rebounded pre-market while retail doesn't budge [237]. That is the crowd's signal: holders are staying put. CNBC's Jim Cramer called Rigetti 'a meme stock' [238], and Investorsobserver asked whether Rigetti is the Nvidia of quantum computing [239]. Leveraged products have arrived: Yahoo Finance lists a Defiance 2X long IonQ ETF under the ticker IONX [240], and Defiance has launched 2X leveraged ETFs on Rocket Lab and Hims & Hers [241]. Yahoo Finance is also running pieces that pit IonQ against Nvidia as an AI stock [242], so the trade is being sold as an AI adjacency.

Historical Analog: The closest analogue is the 2023 Nvidia-led AI run. The mechanics: the bellwether moves first on a story that is credible, institutions buy it, and then a second wave buys the smaller names that carry the same story with more leverage, because they missed the bellwether and want a cheaper ticket. The second wave is what makes the pure plays fall hardest when the story takes a single bad headline. The 1999 infrastructure trade followed the same sequence in networking names, and the 2021 GameStop squeeze showed the same kind of crowd can move a stock far from its fundamentals. Quantum sits in the middle of that sequence: a CEO's comment has already moved the group once [243], and the pure plays now hold the second-wave bid.

Smart Money View: Institutions are split on pace rather than direction. The supportive side is the Quantum Insider's read that analysts see Nvidia's pending Quantum Day as more than a gesture [244], and Finextra's line that quantum computing reaches an inflection point in 2029 [245]. The hedging side is the Microsoft debate: scientists questioned the company's quantum breakthrough [246], and the debate over its Majorana findings continues [247]. IBD's account of the earlier crash that Nvidia's chief executive triggered [243] says the trade has been whipsawed by sentiment. Institutions appear to dispute the timing more than the destination.

When the Narrative Breaks: Watch the price levels. IonQ's 20-session reference is 37.70: a close back above it would end the drawdown narrative, while a close back under 21.82 after the 16.68% rebound would show the bounce failed (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Rigetti's reference is 11.02 and D-Wave's is 5.33, and D-Wave is the only one of the three above its reference. The event risk is Nvidia's pending Quantum Day [244], and the funding risk is visible: IonQ halted its ATM after raising $372M [237]. The instrument risk is leverage. A 2X fund amplifies both legs, so the single-day rebounds and the 20-session drawdowns are magnified for anyone holding the leveraged wrapper [240].

Why Retail Is Here: Nuclear is the cleanest AI-power story the crowd can buy. CNBC reported that Amazon, Google and Meta support tripling nuclear power by 2050 [248], and Alphabet says it aims to slash the cost of new nuclear with small reactor deployments [124]. Stocktwits headlined that NuScale and Oklo surged on the news [249], so the story delivers an instant pop that the crowd can chase.

Where It Breaks: The trigger is in the price. Oklo closed at 26.19 USD, up 2.83% in the prior session but down 47.70% over 20 sessions from 50.08 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). NuScale closed at 15.98, down 1.42% in the session and 38.21% over 20 sessions from 25.86 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Retail sentiment is already turning, as Stocktwits put it when it said sentiment pulled back on the surge [249]. The fundamental question is still open, since Utility Dive wrote that US SMR deals remain elusive for NuScale [250]. A close back above 50.08 would mark the drawdown as over, and the instrument risk is liquidity and single-name concentration in small caps.

Why Retail Is Here: The pitch is simple: Europe is rearming, the money is multi-year, and the stocks look like the tech leaders of the last decade. eToro's headline asks whether European defense is the new Magnificent 7 and says the sector surged 46% year to date while US big tech lagged [251]. Investing.com described European defense stocks as going parabolic as war spending surges [252], and in Warsaw speculators shifted from the Ukrainian names into steel and defense stocks [91].

Where It Breaks: The price is the hurdle. RHM.DE closed at 1,265.00 EUR, up 9.62% in the prior session and 73.76% over 20 sessions from 728.00 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The earnings support is real, since Rheinmetall expects robust 2025 sales [183]. The break is political: the EU exemption for defense spending is still a proposal [20]. The sceptic case is that Europe will not earn much on weapons, as Money.pl quoted the 'lack of world-class products' [253], and Yanis Varoufakis calls rearming Europe the EU's next folly [254]. A close back under 728.00 would show the 20-session move was a reset of the base rather than a trend.

Why Retail Is Here: The meme coin is the crowd's cheapest way in, and the brokers are paying people to play. Robinhood ran a $2M bitcoin and Dogecoin trivia game [255], which drew nearly 400K players to its first $1 million bitcoin trivia game [256], and its HQ Trivia contest put Doge into the prize pool alongside bitcoin [257]. The story the crowd tells is that a dog coin with brokerage distribution can keep a community alive, and a new meme coin from Dogecoin's rights holder [258] is the sign the sponsors want to keep it going.

Where It Breaks: The price is the hurdle. DOGE closed at 0.17 USD, up 5.00% in the prior session but down 32.36% over 20 sessions from 0.25 (Yahoo Finance, prior completed daily close 2025-03-12). Traders are watching $0.16 [259], while a TradingView call sees $2.74 as possible [260]. The cautionary tale is the sponsor coins: President Trump's Solana meme coin is down 85% from its peak [261], and Trump's own meme coin is down 81% since launch [262]. The instrument risk is extreme, and the regulatory line is moving: SEC staff clarified that meme coins are not securities [263]. A reclaim of 0.25, the 20-session reference, is the level that would bring the crowd back, and a break below 0.16 is where the trivia-prize holders would be forced out.

Narrative

Utilities are the power-demand hedge. XLU is down 2.80% over 20 sessions at 77.17 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), but the story is grid demand and the trade war's electricity front. NPR reported the US buys electricity from Canada, which is now a focus of the trade war [[n4886]].
Reported

Ontario slapped a 25% tax increase on electricity exports to the US in response to the trade war [[n4435]], Ontario then suspended its electricity price hikes, and Trump halted the doubling of metals tariffs in response [[n4709]]. Utilities are a political target as well as a grid story.
EPS Upside Watch

Grid capex is the earnings driver. Hitachi Energy committed $250M to address the transformer shortage [[n7859]], and Utility Dive wrote that growing electricity demand needs new policy solutions [[n9238]].
⚡ Breaking Convention

Utilities may subsidize data-centre growth by shifting costs to other ratepayers, a Harvard Law paper argues [[n8138]]. That is a political risk to the regulated return, which cuts against the view of utilities as a bond proxy.
Narrative

European autos are a tariff trade. The iShares European autos ETF is flat over 20 sessions at 52.38 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and automakers are bracing for higher costs as steel and aluminium tariffs kick in [[n9091]]. BMW is up 10.55% over 20 sessions at 84.28 EUR, but it will absorb tariff costs on some Mexican-built models [[n4786]].
Reported

Volkswagen expects 2025 revenue to rise as tariffs loom [[n3056]], but its profit is under pressure from tariffs and competition [[n3057]]. Porsche's earnings per share were cut by a third in 2024 [[n3126]].
EPS Upside Watch

Volkswagen's preferred shares are the upside set-up: up 17.29% over 20 sessions at 109.95 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and the company says revenue grows in 2025 [[n3056]]. The set-up is revenue recovery, not margin recovery.
⚡ Breaking Convention

Volkswagen and Stellantis evaded Trump's 25% tariffs [[n4521]], which cuts against the sector bear case. The bear case still holds on margins, which is why the stance stays bearish while the revenue read is mixed.
Narrative

Semis are split between AI demand and Asian supply competition. SOXX is down 10.83% over 20 sessions at 196.08 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), but gained 2.06% in the prior session. Intel named Lip-Bu Tan chief executive [[n9268]], and Reuters reported TSMC pitched Nvidia, AMD and Broadcom on a foundry joint venture for Intel [[n9164]].
Reported

Marvell's shares tumbled despite strong AI revenue growth [[n3018]], and the stock is down 35.99% over 20 sessions at 69.85 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Nvidia's 30% sell-off has left the shares cheaper than when ChatGPT launched, by one metric [[n6343]].
EPS Upside Watch
Memory is the sharpest upside. Micron is positioned for a prolonged memory cycle [[n3019]], and the stock is up 1.66% over 20 sessions at 95.64 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).
⚡ Breaking Convention

China is building around US chips. Huawei reportedly acquired two million Ascend 910 AI chips from TSMC through shell companies [[n1355]], and a Chinese team won an award for replacing an Nvidia GPU with an industrial chip [[n1548]]. That cuts against the view that US chip leadership is unchallenged.

earnings_pattern.title: Guidance sets the reaction, not the quarter
parts: Rewarded

Rheinmetall expects robust 2025 sales [[n9390]] and sees a profit jump as Europe prepares for a military spending surge [[n9391]]. The stock rose 9.62% in the prior session at 1,265.00 EUR (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Volkswagen's guidance that revenue will rise in 2025 [[n3056]] has its preferred shares up 17.29% over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), and Air France-KLM's shares jumped on an earnings beat and growth expectations [[n2630]]. Both moves came with growth attached rather than cost cuts, which is the pattern the next block is built on.
Punished

Kohl's shares plunged 20% on a rough outlook [[n3013]], and Delta cut its outlook, with the stock falling after the company cited 'macro uncertainty' [[n2980]]. Costco fell 11.52% over five sessions after its quarterly profit missed expectations [[n2776]], and Marvell dropped nearly 20% when its outlook fell short of high expectations [[n2703]], a 22.51% fall over five sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).
Pattern

The sorting variable is guidance, not the quarter. Oracle's sales missed estimates even as its chief executive pointed to AI-driven growth [[n0501]], and Marvell's strong AI revenue growth did not prevent a 35.99% fall over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Consumer names that cut outlooks on tariffs fell hardest, while the one name that guided up on defense demand was rewarded.
Attention into EPS

The next reaction set-up is Nio's fourth-quarter report on March 21 [[n3025]], which will test the China EV read-across after Tesla's trouble in China [[n7597]]. For the US consumer, the Costco and Target reactions set the bar for the next consumer print.
Playbook

Sell the guide, not the beat. Do not buy a stock on a quarter beat when the guidance is cut, and wait for the guidance-driven drawdown to stabilise before adding. Guidance raisers in defense are the funding leg for the sector rotation. The call is invalidated by a second guidance cut in the same sector inside a month.

flows.title: Dip-buying meets de-risking
parts: Global Liquidity

Fed liquidity is on hold, with a cut bias for later. Powell said the Fed is in no hurry to adjust rates [[n11248]], and Reuters reported him signalling possible tweaks to the dot plot [[n11226]]. The Fed's Waller sees cuts this year but not this month [[n11150]]. The ECB published its strategy document, 'A robust strategy for a new era' [[n3572]], and the euro area's inflation worries now run through trade and defense shocks [[n3590]]. In China liquidity is tighter at the margin: a strategist says more Chinese bond issuance, used to keep yields up, will drain liquidity from markets [[n3815]]. The Nasdaq plans 24-hour trading five days a week [[n11240]], a structural change in when liquidity is available. Japan's yen is also the flow of the moment: a strategist calls it the new safe-haven currency [[n5240]].
Rates & Dollar

The 10-year closed at 4.32% (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12), 22 bps lower over 20 observations, and the 2-year at 4.01% fell 28 bps. The dollar index at 103.61 rose 0.16% in the prior session and is 4.03% lower over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). CNBC reports the dollar is rising but remains pressured against peers with tariffs in focus [[n11595]], and The Guardian reports the euro and pound rose against the dollar amid 'Trumpcession' fears [[n3533]]. Duration is the clean hedge: TLT is up 1.62% over 20 sessions at 89.86 and IEF is up 1.67% at 94.43 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).
Credit Check

Credit is where the stress is showing. Bloomberg wrote that a massive unwind makes US junk bonds a riskier bet than Europe's [[n3888]], and Goldman says US credit spreads will get a lot wider amid tariffs [[n3945]]. HYG is down 0.65% over 20 sessions at 78.96 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), while LQD is up 0.32% at 107.66 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). Private-credit wrappers are the new test: Blackstone won SEC approval for an interval fund [[n7708]], and an Australian lender was still gating redemptions [[n6339]].
Equity & Fund Flows

Dip-buying is the flow story. Reuters reported that investors bought a Magnificent 7 ETF amid the downturn [[n6515]]. Hedge funds sped up de-risking, and more is likely to come, Reuters says [[n3946]], while in Europe hedge funds fled positions and dented stock traders [[n3538]]. Millennium's $900 million loss is a sign of broader hedge-fund pain [[n3831]], and Goldman says hedge funds have given up half of their 2025 gains [[n3679]]. Options are the hedge: Moomoo reported put-option volume at a record high [[n11576]]. Retail is buying where institutions are selling: Investment Week reported that wealth managers ditched investment trusts as retail investors bought in droves [[n6382]], and Italy's asset managers saw net inflows double to 6 billion euros in February [[n3885]]. Buybacks are arriving at the small end, with Metropolitan Bank announcing a $50 million repurchase [[n3955]].
Portfolio Implication

Hold duration through TLT and IEF as the hedge, keep the dollar exposure tactical, and buy equity protection with puts while put volume is at a record. Avoid high-yield beta until HYG reclaims its 20-session reference of 79.48 (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12). The portfolio change is to move from credit carry into Treasuries, and to add risk only after a clean stopgap vote and a steadier VIX. Currency hedges matter too: yen strength is the transmission channel to watch if the BOJ moves toward a May hike [[n5195]], and it would hit the Japanese equity leg.

anticipatory.title: The shutdown vote and the VIX
parts: What Is Priced

The market is pricing a political scare, not a fiscal break. The House passed a stopgap [[n11597]], and Senate Democrats are fuming as the shutdown deadline nears [[n11598]]. House leaders are holding their lines ahead of the vote [[n11335]]. The S&P 500 is down 7.73% over 20 sessions, while the VIX at 24.23 is up 51.25% over the same span (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12).
Conditional Expression

If the Senate passes the stopgap, the VIX should retrace toward its 16.02 reference and the equity drawdown should stop extending, with the trade shifting back to tariffs. If the Senate balks, the shutdown premium holds, the VIX stays elevated, and the Treasury rally carries on as the hedge.
Risk

The near-term damage falls on federal workers: Axios reported that the chaos will delay unemployment benefits for federal workers and the states [[n11066]]. The bigger risk is a stopgap that passes while the tariff calendar stays unresolved.

anticipatory.title: The April 2 tariff step
parts: What Is Priced

Tariff timing is what the market is pricing. Mexico will not pay tariffs on USMCA goods until April 2, Trump said [[n4051]], and the auto industry is pleading for trade certainty as April 2 tariffs loom [[n4145]]. Canada will impose 25% reciprocal tariffs following US steel and aluminium duties [[n9119]], and Trump halted the plan to double Canadian metal tariffs to 50% [[n9491]].
Conditional Expression

If the tariff step set for April 2 proceeds [[n4145]], the auto and steel exposure in the European and Japanese names takes the cost hit first, which is why the autos stance stays bearish. If it is delayed again, the tariff premium fades in the Canadian and Mexican names and the VIX drifts back toward its reference.
Risk

The pattern is the risk. Trump has delayed and reversed tariffs in the window, with CNN reporting a one-month delay on tariffs for Mexico and Canada [[n4090]], so each reversal re-prices volatility rather than resolving it.

anticipatory.title: The March Fed pause and the dot plot
parts: What Is Priced

A cut is priced for later in the year, not this month. The Fed's Waller sees cuts this year but not this month [[n11150]], and Powell said the Fed is in no hurry to adjust rates [[n11248]]. The curve has already moved: the 2-year is down 28 bps over 20 observations and the 10-year down 22 bps (US Treasury, prior close 2025-03-12).
Conditional Expression

If the March pause is confirmed and the dot plot stays unchanged, the front end holds its gains and the bull steepening continues. If the Fed signals a higher-for-longer path, the 2-year gives back its 28 bps and the curve flattens, which is the bank-margin bear case.
Risk

Powell's comments left the forecast framework in play: Reuters reported him signalling possible tweaks to the dot plot of rate-path forecasts [[n11226]], so the next set of projections could move the market more than the decision itself.

anticipatory.title: German spending and the defense exemption

The market is pricing a German fiscal impulse with a defense carve-out. EU ministers back a temporary exemption for defense spending from the bloc's rules [[n5494]], and Merz has two weeks to deliver a historic spending revolution [[n3412]]. The DAX is up 2.39% over 20 sessions while the STOXX Europe 600 is down 1.19% (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12), so Germany is running ahead of the region.
Conditional Expression

If the package passes on schedule, defense and infrastructure supply chains keep leading and the Bund curve steepens. If it stalls, the rally fades back toward the 20-session base, and the euro's 5.30% gain over 20 sessions (Yahoo Finance, prior close 2025-03-12) gives back ground.
Risk

Inflation and supply are the risks. Lagarde warned higher defense spending could push inflation up [[n3583]], and Reuters flagged that German spending surge worries loom over the Bund market [[n3528]]. The Bundesbank called the spending justified but not a cure-all [[n3501]].
